_meta.title: Web Application Attacks
_meta.description: The modern frontier: the vuln classes that own the public internet, from server-side request forgery to logic abuse. Every technique here is taught end-to-end for free in PortSwigger's Academy, and every one has a first-class fix.

techniques.name: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
techniques.summary: Make the server issue requests of your choosing: hit cloud metadata (169.254.169.254 - instant IAM credentials), pivot into internal-only services, scan the RFC1918 space from inside. The cloud-era killer because the metadata endpoint hands over role credentials to anyone who can make the host talk to itself.

detection.description: Egress logs from app tier to link-local/metadata addresses, DNS for internal hostnames initiated by app processes, unusual URL schemes in request parameters (file://, gopher://), WAF rules for metadata IPs, canary tokens on metadata endpoints.
mitigations: IMDSv2 (token-required, hop-limit) on all cloud instances - the definitive metadata fix
Egress allowlists from app tier (default deny to RFC1918 + link-local)
URL validation against allowlist schemes/hosts; never accept raw URLs from users
Separate network zones so app compromise does not equal internal reach

techniques.name: Path Traversal & Local File Inclusion
techniques.summary: Read (and sometimes execute) arbitrary files by walking out of a sanitized path: ../../../etc/passwd, encoded variants (%2e%2e%2f), PHP filters (php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=index), null bytes in legacy parsers. LFI plus log poisoning or session files crosses into RCE.

detection.description: WAF traversal-pattern rules, application errors revealing file paths, anomalous access to /etc/, win.ini, web.config from app logs, high volume of 200s on deep-dot segments, php:// filter strings in access logs.
mitigations: Never build paths from user input - map IDs to fixed paths server-side (the real fix)
Chroot/containerize file access for the app user
Deny-list directories at the web server layer as a second wall
Least-privilege service accounts (can't read what the account can't read)

techniques.name: Authentication & Session Logic Abuse
techniques.summary: The soft, high-yield class: broken session validation (predictable tokens, missing rotation on privilege change), mass assignment to role fields, JWT alg=none/key confusion, reset-link enumeration, 2FA logic gaps (response manipulation, brute-forceable OTP windows, missing step-up). Rarely toolable - it is reasoning work, which is exactly why it survives.

detection.description: Login-success anomalies per account (impossible-travel, new-ASN), session token reuse across IPs, JWT validation errors in app logs, password-reset bursts against one account from distributed sources, 2FA-step error-rate anomalies.
mitigations: Framework auth (battle-tested) over hand-rolled; deny-by-default route guards
Session rotation on login AND privilege change; short lifetimes; secure flags
JWT: strict alg allowlist, aud/iss validation, short exp
Rate-limit and alert on reset flows; number-linked OTP validation server-side

techniques.name: Race Conditions & Cache Poisoning
techniques.summary: Race the server's check-then-act windows with synchronized requests (HTTP/2 single-packet racing made this practical: 20 requests in one packet), or poison a shared cache by smuggling an unkeyed header (X-Forwarded-Host, X-Original-URL) so every subsequent user receives your payload. Web-cache poisoning is site-wide impact from a single request.

detection.description: Request-burst analytics (identical requests within one server tick), duplicate-resource errors (double-spend signatures in payment logs), cache-content drift (same URL serving different bodies to different users), header-anomaly WAF rules.
mitigations: Idempotency keys and DB unique constraints (the race's real fix)
Cache: minimize keyed-header deviations, Vary correctly, prefix cache keys with host
H2/H3 connection-window limits server-side; normalize duplicate headers
Surrogate-control discipline; cache-purge runbooks

techniques.name: Client-Side Web Attacks (XSS / CSRF / Prototype Pollution)
techniques.summary: Attacks that run in the victim's browser: stored/reflected XSS (script executes with the victim's privileges), CSRF (cross-site state-change on authenticated sessions), and DOM/prototype pollution (JS gadget chains in frameworks like jQuery/Lodash). XSS is the gateway to session theft, keylogging, and same-origin pivoting.

detection.description: DOM sandbox alerts, CSP violation reports (a real telemetry source), WAF script-tag payloads, unexpected outbound connections to user-controlled domains from browsers, account-activity anomalies following reported phishing.
mitigations: CSP with nonces (defeats inline XSS) + trusted-types for DOM sinks
Output encoding by context (HTML/attr/JS/URL) via templating engines
SameSite=Lax/Strict cookies + CSRF tokens on state-changing routes
Prototype pollution: freeze Object.prototype in sensitive apps, audit deep-merge libraries

techniques.name: Broken Access Control (IDOR / BOLA)
techniques.summary: The server asks 'does this session exist' but never 'does this session OWN this object' - so /api/invoices/1043 becomes /api/invoices/1044 and another tenant's data walks out. IDOR at object level (BOLA in the OWASP API Top 10), forced-browse at function level, parameter tampering for privilege lifts. Consistently ranked the #1 real-world web risk because it needs no payload, no injection break, no crash - just a horizontal walk an authorization layer never checked. Mostly read-class, which is why it escapes blast-radius gating while still being the quietest data breach in the catalog.

detection.description: Application logs must capture session-user AND accessed object-id, then correlate: one session touching a wide, distinct set of object ids is enumeration; canary objects (honey-records with unique ids per user) turn IDOR into a certain-signal tripwire; WSTG 4.1 authorization test matrix run in CI catches the class pre-deploy; API-gateway anomaly on 200-with-foreign-object patterns where the app logs both fields.
mitigations: Deny-by-default server-side authorization per object - never trust client-supplied object ownership
Framework-level scoping: ORM row-level filters instead of view-level checks
Per-role integration tests that assert both allow AND deny paths
Non-guessable object ids (UUIDv4+) as friction, never as the control
